caption_hook: Maine has been a drowned coast, a forest of the first land plants and a sea of molten granite.

layers.name: PRESUMPSCOT CLAY
layers.what: When the ice sheet melted, the ocean flooded the pressed-down land and laid gray clay along the coast. The land then rebounded, lifting that sea-floor mud high above today's shoreline.
layers.bonus: Seashells turn up in these clays far inland, well above present sea level.

layers.name: TROUT VALLEY FORMATION
layers.what: River sand and mud buried early land plants near today's Mount Katahdin. Their stems and spores, still found in this rock, show what the first plant-covered landscapes looked like.
layers.bonus: Pertica quadrifaria, a leafless plant from this rock, is Maine's official state fossil.

layers.name: KATAHDIN GRANITE
layers.what: Molten rock cooled into granite beneath older rock. Glaciers later scraped the surrounding land away, leaving Mount Katahdin standing as a bare granite peak 5,269 feet high.
layers.bonus: Katahdin is the northern end of the Appalachian Trail, which runs more than 2,000 miles.

layers.name: CADILLAC GRANITE
layers.hook: The pink granite of the coast
layers.what: Magma cooled slowly under Mount Desert Island into pink granite. The great ice sheet later scoured it, rounding the peaks and carving the bays of Acadia National Park.
layers.bonus: At 1,530 feet, Cadillac Mountain is the tallest peak on the U.S. Atlantic coast.

layers.name: THE BASEMENT
layers.what: In the western mountains, a block of gneiss and granite called the Chain Lakes Massif holds some of Maine's oldest known rock. It was welded onto North America during ancient plate collisions.
layers.bonus: Plate collisions carried this fragment in from far away before the Appalachians rose.
